# Judith Chapter 13 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)

**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Vaticanus, Judith 13 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/JDT_013_page_001.jpg

---

**1** As evening fell, his servants cleared out quickly. Bagoas closed the tent from outside and sent the attendants away from his master's presence. They trudged off to their beds — every one of them exhausted after the long banquet.

**2** Judith was alone in the tent. Holofernes lay on his bed, drowned in wine.

**3** She had already told her servant to wait outside the bedchamber and watch for her to come out, as she did every night. She had told Bagoas the same thing: she was going out to pray.

**4** Everyone was gone. No one remained in the bedchamber — not great, not small. Judith stood beside his bed and prayed silently to her heart: "O LORD God of all power — look down now, in this hour, upon the work of my hands. Do it for the exaltation of Jerusalem.

**5** Now is the time to help your inheritance. Now is the time to accomplish what I have come for — the destruction of the enemies who have risen against us."

**6** She crossed the tent to the bedpost at Holofernes' head. His sword hung there. She lifted it down.

**7** She stepped to the bed. She took hold of the hair of his head.

"Give me strength, O LORD God of Israel, this day."

**8** She struck his neck with all her might — once, twice — and cut off his head.

**9** She rolled his body from the bed. She pulled down the canopy from its posts. A moment later, she walked out and pressed the head of Holofernes into her servant's hands.

**10** The servant put it in the food bag. And the two of them walked out together, just as they did every night for prayer. They passed through the camp, wound around the valley, climbed the mountain of Bethulia, and came to its gates.

**11** From a distance, Judith called out to the sentries at the gate: "Open the gate! Open it! God — our God — is with us! He is still showing his power in Israel, his might against our enemies — just as he did today!"

**12** When the men of the city heard her voice, they came running down to the gate. They sent for the city elders.

**13** Everyone came — old and young — because her return was not expected. They opened the gate and let them in. They lit torches. They crowded around her.

**14** And she cried out, loud enough for all to hear:

"Praise God — praise him! Praise God, who never withdrew his mercy from the house of Israel — who shattered our enemies by my hand, this very night!"

**15** She reached into the bag and pulled out the head and held it up before them.

"Look. The head of Holofernes — supreme commander of the Assyrian army. And look — the canopy he was lying under when he was drunk. The LORD struck him by the hand of a woman."

**16** "As the LORD lives — he who kept me safe every step of the way I walked — it was my face that led him to his ruin. He never touched me. He never defiled me. My honor is untouched."

**17** The people were staggered. They fell to their knees and bowed their faces to the ground and worshiped God together with one voice: "Blessed are you, our God, who this day have brought shame upon the enemies of your people!"

**18** Then Uzziah spoke to her: "Blessed are you, daughter — blessed above all women on the face of the earth. And blessed be the LORD God, creator of heaven and earth, who directed your hand to cut off the head of the chief of our enemies.

**19** Your hope will never leave human hearts as long as they remember the power of God — forever."

**20** "May God make what you have done an everlasting honor to you. May he come to you with his blessings — because you did not spare yourself when our people were brought low. You acted against our destruction. You walked the straight path before our God."

And all the people answered: **"Amen! Amen!"**

---
*PNEUMA notes: The pivot of the entire book is in v. 8. PNEUMA presents it with stark brevity — short sentences, hard stops. "Once, twice." No adjectives on the action itself. The horror and the heroism are allowed to speak without ornamentation. The canopy (v. 15) is brought out along with the head as evidence and trophy — two proofs of the deed. Judith's declaration in v. 16 is as important to the narrative as the execution itself: she is announcing that she is clean, that she remained pure, that God protected her from violation. This is not an afterthought. It is the vindication of her honor and her faithfulness.*
